analysis.one_liner: Puts environmental protection first before allowing any new offshore oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee and a subcommittee on June 30, 2010, and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Written in the months after the BP Deepwater Horizon spill, the bill would rewrite federal offshore drilling law so that protecting the marine and coastal environment comes ahead of rapid oil and gas development. It would let drilling proceed only where the Interior Secretary finds, using sound science, that risks are minimal, safety rules are strict, and oil spills can actually be contained. It would also bar drilling entirely from ecologically important areas of the outer Continental Shelf.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, commercial and recreational fishermen, and people whose jobs and health depend on clean coastal waters would benefit from stricter safety findings and permanent protection of ecologically important areas. Taxpayers would also benefit from lower risk of paying cleanup costs and economic damage from a major offshore spill like the one the bill responds to.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities, fishermen, and beach tourism

how_it_helps.text: Reverses the existing statutory policy that favors expeditious development, making protection and maintenance of the marine and coastal environment the primary consideration before any leasing.

Allows offshore oil and gas leasing, exploration, and development only if the Interior Secretary has an environmental baseline and finds, based on sound science, that risks are minimal, rigorous safety measures are in place and enforced, and there is a demonstrated ability to respond to accidents in real-world conditions.

Prohibits including in a leasing program any area with distinguishing ecological characteristics or that contributes disproportionately to ecosystem health, including habitat for endangered or threatened species, so those areas could not be offered for drilling at all.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies would face new preconditions before drilling, permanent exclusion from ecologically important areas, and in some cases denial of access to leases they might otherwise obtain, which could reduce domestic oil and gas production and the royalties and revenue that come with it.

drawbacks.text: The bill would allow drilling only in 'limited areas' where risks are minimal, which oil and gas producers and their allies argued would cut domestic production and increase reliance on imported oil.

The prohibition on any ecologically important area is written broadly enough to cover large parts of the outer Continental Shelf, so the bill would sharply restrict where drilling could ever occur rather than simply add safety rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill responds to a real and recent disaster: the Deepwater Horizon spill showed that drilling could proceed without a proven ability to contain a blowout, and the cleanup, ecological damage, and losses to fishing and tourism communities were enormous. The tradeoff is reduced access for oil and gas companies to large parts of the outer Continental Shelf, and potentially less domestic production. Weighing those, the bill favors people who live, work, and fish along the coasts; its cost falls mainly on one industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Natural Resources Committee, then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, and sat there until Congress ended in January 2011 with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 30, 2010, by Rep. Mike Quigley with two cosponsors, both Democrats.
On the day of introduction it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources, and on July 6, 2010, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources.
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas companies are better off, because the restrictions were never enacted and the existing pro-development statutory policy remained in place. Coastal communities did not gain the protections the bill proposed, but the bill was so narrow in support that the status quo was likely to continue regardless.

for.name: Rep. Mike Quigley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 30, 2010, to make environmental protection the primary factor in offshore drilling decisions.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee / Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over offshore drilling law
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Doc Hastings
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee where the bill was referred, never scheduled action on it.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democrats were involved (the sponsor plus two cosponsors), and the Republican-controlled committee calendar was where the bill stopped; no Republican supported it.

industries.note: The bill would impose preconditions on every lease — sound-science findings on minimal risk, enforced safety measures, and demonstrated spill response — and bar drilling from ecologically important areas, cutting access to offshore resources. Keeping those restrictions off the books preserves the industry's existing access and the pro-development statutory policy.

Permanent protection of ecologically important shelf areas and stricter spill-response findings would protect the fisheries, beaches, and coastal economies that absorb the damage when a spill happens.
